name: Declinism
description: People can read the present as evidence of decline because the past gets remembered more selectively or nostalgically than it really was. “Things are getting worse” can feel like a plain observation when it is partly driven by memory and exposure bias.
design_relevance_note: Relevant to redesign backlash, product nostalgia, community-health narratives, AI/social-media discourse, and organizational retrospectives. Teams can overtrust stories of platform or societal decline relative to an idealized baseline they never measured cleanly.
myth_risk_note: Declinism is poorly operationalized in the empirical literature reviewed here. Most candidates conflate real historical/institutional decline (church attendance, species decline) with the cognitive bias of overstating or over-perceiving decline -- only Elchardus & Spruyt (2014) directly measure perceived-decline attitudes as a social-psychological construct, and the existing corpus's core empirical test (Mastroianni's illusion-of-moral-decline work) remains the primary direct evidence for the bias itself.
prevalence_note: Narratives of decline are common, but the exact label “declinism” is still rare in product/design practice; it appears mostly in tech/media critique, cultural commentary, or unusually reflective strategy discussions.

findings.description: A large survey of the Dutch-speaking Belgian population (N=2,330) found that support for populist political propositions was driven foremost by declinism -- a very negative view of society's evolution -- and by a feeling of unfair group treatment, rather than by personal economic hardship or life dissatisfaction. Establishes declinism as a measurable, real social-perception construct with a genuine downstream political consequence, complementing this corpus's existing illusion-of-moral-decline evidence with a different angle: a real-world attitudinal/political correlate, not a direct test of whether the perceived decline itself is an accurate or inaccurate reading of history.
findings.source_title: Populism, Persistent Republicanism and Declinism: An Empirical Analysis of Populism as a Thin Ideology

findings.description: Across archival and original data totaling 12,492,983 observations from at least 60 nations, people consistently believed morality was declining even though reports of contemporaries' morality did not show a matching decline. The paper argues this perceived decline can be generated by biased exposure to negative information and biased memory for the past.
findings.effect_size: n = 12,492,983 across archival and original studies
